Despite the considerable advancements, these systems still struggle with text comprehension, essentially treating text as data rather than knowledge. We introduce a novel text representation framework inspired by human memory, acknowledging that text is declarative and would benefit from structural organization to facilitate efficient computation. We utilize long-term episodic memory to store text information accumulated over time, maintaining this knowledge in an organized manner, similar to human memory. To simulate human memory capabilities, we incorporated features mimicking short- and long-term memory, as well as an attention mechanism. We also designed an episodic memory module to store text information, differentiating it from the sparse external memory often used in automated memory systems. Furthermore, we propose an iterative method for updating the memory graph, mimicking forgetting and memory retrieval processes common in human psychology. We also propose an alternative graph retrieval approach, utilizing path prediction, to improve recall of irrelevant text items. We evaluate our framework, episodic memory for automated systems, and compare it to multiple existing computational models, specifically those representing human memory and attention in both experimental and observational studies. We also conduct thorough assessments of our framework, specifically updating the memory graph and retrieving memories, to ensure our approach is on the right path.

millimeter-wave systems have received little attention in the design of hybrid precoders. To fill this gap, we develop the first integrated design of analog transmit precoders and digital receive combiners for multicasting in mmWave systems, with each device having multiple phases and multiple antennas. By combining semidefinite relaxation, alternating optimization and Cholesky decomposition, we sequentially optimize the digital and analog components at the transmitter and receivers. Experimental evidence sets upper limits on dielectric loss tangents, approximately $100$ parts-per-billion, however this information comes from fabricated devices with multiple factors contributing to loss.  Our research provides an independent experimental assessment of dielectric loss by analyzing inductive magnetic coupling between qubits and coils.  We observed no significant change in the dielectric loss of high-quality silicon nitride films when used in qubits versus resonators over $100$ times smaller in size, suggesting minimal additional loss during film transfer and mounting.  This finding leads to the conclusion that mean-field dielectric loss terms are negligible, and dielectric loss occurs primarily through variable trap-related mechanisms in high-quality silicon nitride films.  Our data further demonstrates that high-quality silicon nitride films demonstrate thermal stability of dielectric loss at a constant up to $105$ Kelvin, providing a framework to design next-generation two-qubit devices with improved performance.  Finally, we observed no adverse effects of film thickness on the density of trap-related loss sites, providing insight into the design of high-performing silicon nitride qubits for future applications.

, known as the promise set disjointness problem, holds crucial importance in numerous applications. The scenario revolves around k players with subsets S1 through Sk, all containing elements from a set J. Contracting on a random element r from set J, each player receives a portion of set Sr, consisting of elements from subset r. The objective is to determine if the sets' elements form a complete and consistent picture of the set J's elements. The issue can be resolved through a query, asking each participant if their portion of the set r contains a specific element. The success of this approach depends on the number of requests, potentially reaching O(k * |J|), though it's clear a sublinear, o(k * |J|), solution would be preferable. The question remains whether this improved solution exists. The two-point majority (TPM) protocol provides a non-trivial, 2 * |J|, solution, but it's unclear if this solution can be reduced to a single, o(2 * |J|), query. The TPM protocol's fundamental idea revolves around choosing a random subset, consisting of exactly two elements from set J. If the chosen subset's elements appear in sufficient numbers of sets, the sets form a complete and consistent picture of the set J's elements. The issue here is to determine if this idea's validity can be proven or disproven using the set disjointness problem's properties, thus, having a direct impact on the problem's solution.

We have identified the optimal value of the modular inclination angle as being slightly greater than 45 degrees, which provides the maximum possible total effective area in a given sky coverage area. This relationship along with the optimal inclination angle have been incorporated into a multi-objective optimization algorithm to obtain the best design parameters for the COSIMA mission. The algorithm was able to yield solutions that strike a balance between achieving the maximum possible total effective area and minimizing the number of mirror shells, as well as meeting the requirement for uniform sky coverage. The final design of the COSIMA mission consists of 45 partially tilted mirror shells, and we anticipate that this arrangement will enable the mission to cover a large area of the sky while maintaining a high total effective area.

The Set-Union Knapsack Problem involves set functions, while the Budgeted Maximum Coverage Problem uses a linear relaxation of the set function. Despite sharing these attributes, solving one variation does not necessarily provide a solution that is efficient for the other variation. Therefore, directly adapting existing solvers without modification is unlikely to yield a solution, and a reformulation of the problem is required. This paper explores two specific modifications: generalizing item values to weights and splitting items, and applying the greedy algorithm in different orders. Our experimental analysis using the original LSAT test suite reveals that the current best solvers for the Set-Union Knapsack Problem cannot be used without modification to solve the Budgeted Maximum Coverage Problem effectively. However, splitting items and applying the greedy algorithm after splitting items yields the best results, even though the current best solution is still an incomplete result due to early stopping at a specific iteration.

the availability of simple mathematical solutions dwindles, prompting the need for alternative methods. Monte Carlo simulations serve as an intermediary between complicated mathematical formulas and applicable predictions through random sampling. Traditional techniques for generating samples from Gaussian process posterior calculations consider samples as separate draws from the distribution of process values at fixed points. This focus on distribution characteristics leads to strategies that increase exponentially with the desired dimensionality. This becomes impractical for larger datasets, prompting us to consider a new line of thinking, where Gaussian conditionals are viewed in the context of individual data points as random variables. This alternative interpretation yields simpler computational strategies, particularly in the context of non-Gaussian data models that incorporate likelihood functions. Recent investigations heavily rely on statistical techniques such as multivariate analysis, often using a linear model which assumes consistent statistical dependencies across various ENSO phases, a premise not significantly influenced by the two flavors of ENSO (EP and CP types). Consequently, statistical techniques have successfully accurately predicted the two flavors of ENSO with comparable performance. Furthermore, advancements in deep learning methods like Long-Short Term Memory (LSTM) have led to enhanced precision in ENSO flavor prediction. These predictive methods utilize attributes such as multivariate time series from observational datasets or reanalysis, but the underlying techniques assume that data from different sources exhibit consistent properties, a premise verified for ENSO (but not extensively studied for its two flavors). In this research, we focus on utilizing LSTM networks to predict the two flavors of ENSO, but this time directly predicting the two flavors from their initial negative phase. By doing so, we avoid assumptions about features and focus solely on predicting the two flavors, a approach which proves highly challenging due to the predicted variables being part of a larger, highly variable and nonlinear high-dimensional dataset. In a surprising development, we prove that accurately predicting the two flavors is highly linked to a previously unresolved problem in mathematics - solving $x\sin(x) - x^3 = -0.00016$ - a result previously unexplored in any research paper until now.

to investigate turbulent transport properties, where the flow field statistics are represented as a continuous time Markov process. This representation accurately captures turbulence's essence, where the average velocity field appears as a stationary Gaussian process. As a practical example, we use the orbital advection of droplets in a finite 2D box to illustrate the Markovian modeling approach. For small droplet sizes, the probability density function (PDF) of the velocity field resolves perfectly, complying with the Gaussian statistics. However, for sufficiently large droplets, turbulent effects emerge, and the velocity field's PDF exhibits non-Gaussian features. Notably, the PDF displays asymmetry and statisitcal moment negations, characteristic of Gaussian-delta function (Gaussian $\delta$) mixtures. Furthermore, we find that the mean square velocity fluctuation satisfies the Kolmogorov's two-thirds law. By introducing a large droplet into the system, we perform a quantitative evaluation of turbulent transport and find that the effective diffusion coefficient can be represented as the product of the mean square area and the mean flow velocity, divided by the mean path length.

Employing a spherical projection technique to transform point clouds into a unified format, our approach recognizes common objects within a standardized image and relies on a novel geometric distribution model to create a recognizable placeholder. Experimental results conducted on the NuScenes and Baidu Apollo dataset demonstrate the proposed algorithm's superior recall and efficiency over existing state-of-the-art place recognition techniques.

iferromagnetism and nematic order in iron-based superconductors is still the subject of controversy. A recent study of these structures focused on the expected weight distribution, specifically the variance, under a given condition. In this work, we explore the variance of the weight of a minimum spanning tree in a random graph and establish two key findings. First, for graphs with a minimum spanning tree of small weight and following a geometric distribution, the variance satisfies a specific equation and is related to the average weight. This finding is analogous to a known theorem for variances in graph theory and indicates the variance is smaller than the square of the average weight. Second, when the variance is averaged, it satisfies an equation resembling a known differential equation from another field of study. We also demonstrate that our results can be extended to the minimum spanning acycle in simplicial complexes and show the average variance converges to a known value when a particular control factor is adjusted. The study was made possible by the existence of a normal limit distribution for the weight of a minimum spanning tree and its relationship to variances in graph theory.

iu:2019xhn}, we examine the prospect of primordial black holes emerging from the second inflationary process caused by the dark matter field. It is assumed that the dark matter field undergoes a high-scale inflationary process. When the dark matter field reaches the cutoff of its potential, it experiences a sudden oscillation, resulting in the creation of a vast number of black holes. We employ the multi-messenger approach to calculate the production of primordial black holes and their potential contribution to dark matter, incorporating recent constraints. The findings indicate that the estimated production of black holes may be significantly reduced due to constraints on high-scale inflation, but there are still some possibilities where the production can exceed the forecast based on density measurements. Furthermore, our analysis shows that the estimated mass of black holes, influenced by the inflation potential and dark matter coupling constants, may be below $10^{16}$-$10^{17}$ grams in some possible scenarios, offering a distinct property that differentiates this scenario from others proposing high-scale inflation.

grasp and manipulate objects is an essential yet complex challenge. In comparison to other object-grasping fields, dexterous grasping has been understudied, mainly due to a shortage of extensive datasets. To address this issue, our study introduces DexGraspNet - a large-scale simulated dataset - designed specifically for robotic dexterous grasping, paired with an approach to achieve highly diverse synthesis. By utilizing a combined approach of multi-task learning and diversity training with a novel objective function, our methods can successfully allow a trained classifier to generate diverse, robust, and transferable grasping configurations, which perform better compared to previous approaches. Sketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (with the largest squared magnitude) of a given vector. However, the CountSketch sketch falls short in situations where subsequent vectors rely on feedback from previous inputs. Under such circumstances, the classic estimator can be compromised by a relatively low number of inferences, essentially making it vulnerable to manipulation. A more resilient estimator was proposed, which, albeit requiring quadratically more queries in proportion to the sketch size, significantly enhances the safety by a factor of k (with k being the number of key components) when compared to the initial estimator.

The program's current implementation has been adapted for the following languages: python, c, and cuda, and it can be run on the cluster and in the cluster node, with the average of the electron-boson-holon configuration sampling taking around 5-10 nanoseconds per step. From the seller's perspective, we explore two key objectives: maximizing revenue and setting a minimum auction price to guarantee a target profit. From the buyers' perspective, we investigate the effectiveness of bid strategies in achieving optimal bids and protecting their private valuations when participating in such auctions. Our study identifies the conditions under which an auction design can simultaneously maximize revenue and ensure sealed bids are optimal not only for the buyer but also for other potential valuations. We highlight an important class of auctions that can simultaneously achieve optimal revenue and protected individual valuations for unit-demand buyers. Specifically, we show that a simple lowest-second price auction performs well in generating optimal revenue and preserving individual privacy, making it a robust solution. Additionally, we show that using a knapsack auction approach allows the seller to set a lower price while still maintaining individual privacy for the buyers. A key finding reveals that robust individual privacy cannot coexist with optimal revenue when dealing with unit-demand buyers, unless the auction is designed to encourage buyers to participate with minimal effort in auction bidding.

This study examines the correlation between human voice peaks and the peaks of the neural signals of two primary brain areas involved in language processing in individuals with typical and atypical language development. We utilized a novel approach to investigate the relationship between speech syllable peaks and the peaks of the brain signals in two language-processing areas in the brain, and employed a novel measure to analyze the synergetic behavior between the brain regions. Our results indicate a statistically significant link between syllable peak frequencies in speech and the early response peaks in the left Broca's area in typical and atypical populations, as well as significant correlations between syllable peaks and the late response peaks in the left Broca's area and right temporal cortex in typical populations. Our findings highlight the distinct ways in which typical and atypical populations utilize brain language signals, and emphasize the importance of considering syllable structure information when developing language intervention interventions.

we studied a distant starburst galaxy, examining how star formation-driven gas outflows are linked to other properties of the galaxy. Our data show a nearly linear relationship between outflow mass and star formation rates, as well as a significant correlation between outflow mass and gas usage times. In regions of high star formation rates within the galaxy, the mass ejected through outflows exceeds the amount of gas converted into new stars, indicating that outflows could limit the galaxy's star formation. Our findings support other studies indicating that outflows can regulate the galaxy's gas usage, while the observed relationships between outflows and star formation properties may be influenced by how efficiently the outflows transport gas out of the galaxy.

Euler characteristic is a fundamental, widely recognized topological invariant with numerous past uses in data analysis. Our primary objective is to illustrate its applicability in analyzing datasets employing categorical labels. As a foundational topological invariant, Euler characteristic has two distinct expressions - one based on homology, and the other, preferred by the community, uses simplicial decompositions. This paper employs the second method to demonstrate Euler characteristic's capabilities when dealing with labeled data. To showcase its utility, we apply the constructed diagrams to investigate multi-variable dose-response models. Dose-response models, a vital aspect of systems medicine, describe how biological systems react to external factors or treatments. In this context, our application of Euler characteristic showcases its potential for data analysis in multi-variable spaces using categorical labels, thereby offering a structured framework for exploring complex datasets.

However, the time-variation of these quasistationary states when the external drive is continuous, especially when the drive depends on time in a complex way, poses significant challenges to understanding the Floquet picture, especially when the drive is said to be weak. We first describe this finding using a perturbative approach, then provide a non-perturbative explanation, revealing that these quasistationary changes are a common characteristic of ergodic systems driven continuously. This study explores how these two nonclassical traits are connected in the context of remotely generating Wigner negativity with entanglement-assisted protocols, focusing on quantum correlations as a resource. We analyze a scenario where two parties, A and B, share a Wigner-function-transformed state and utilize the hot-bit scenario to determine which party, A or B, can generate Wigner negativity in party A by receiving hot bits from party B, as well as the optimal probability of event occurrence to maximize this effect. We find that the total success probability is directly related to the quantum correlation quantifier, specifically the relative entropy of entanglement, enabling us to establish the Wigner-function-transformed state's exact amount of relative entropy of entanglement and provide the asymptotic stability of this quantity under local operations and classical communication. This findings extend to other scenarios, including the cold-bit scenario and the scenario where Wigner-function transformation occurs in party B. We also demonstrate that the total success probability is directly related to the amount of quantum correlation in the system, which is also asymptotically stable for certain protocols.

This study aims to develop a novel and flexible approach to detecting anomalies in subgraphs by creating a subspace dictionary using a graph-based kernelized principal component analysis. The graph-based kernelized principal component analysis is an extension of traditional kernelized principal component analysis, incorporating graph-based kernel methods to consider the structural information of graphs. This allows us to apply graph-based kernel methods to unsupervised anomaly detection in graphs. The graph-based kernel methods project graph data into a higher dimension to capture intrinsic structure characteristics, improving detection performance. Our method first transforms given graph data into a weighted kernel matrix, then performs principal component analysis to find the best-fitting subgraph for each data point. Anomalous samples are identified by measuring their distance from the projected subspace and selecting data points that fall beyond a threshold from the original space. The efficacy of our method is evaluated through various numerical experiments and real-world applications. Our method achieves superior anomaly detection compared to existing methods, demonstrating its effectiveness and versatility. The approach and associated implementation can be easily applied to a wide range of graph-based kernels without needing significant modifications. While believed to hold for all processes, Bayes' rule leads to inconsistencies in Quantum Mechanics when applied to certain situations such as Frauchiger-Renner's paradox. Similar issues also occur in the Hardy setup, despite treating Quantum Mechanics as a non-local theory. To resolve these inconsistencies, an input-output causal relation, based on a modified version called quantum Bayes' rule, is formulated for quantum processes, particularly benefiting from the principles of no-signalling and contextuality. Quantum Bayes' rule serves as an accurate representation of this relation and is proven to be consistent within the framework of Quantum Mechanics, effectively generalizing Bayes' rule for quantum systems, just as it applies to classical, stochastic processes.

Entity Typing (FG-NET) is to accurately classify various entity types, often exceeding hundreds, by considering the context of each mention. However, the common approach to acquire supervised training data through distant supervision introduces label noise by assigning type labels without considering the context. In order to mitigate this issue, FG-NET research adopts a simplified model that factors in entity context, often employing a limited number of features. As the entity context plays a vital role in achieving better performance in FG-NET, we are proposing a new context-focused module called Context-aware Typing Memory (CTM), incorporating both short and long-term memory contexts near each mention. This module also aims to decrease data noise by representing the memory context through self-supervised contrastive learning. We evaluate our proposed CTM module in comparison to multiple baseline models, including those involving the massive unsupervised FG-NET dataset in News articles. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed CTM module significantly outperforms the benchmark models, also surpassing previously established supervised FG-NET models when applied to unsupervised datasets.

centers largely relies on load balancing, and virtualization enables this by using a dynamic load scheduler. However, these schedulers have reached their limits as data center load has continued to rise, and the predictability of scheduling is crucial for the effectiveness of online scheduling techniques. In this research, a novel load scheduling approach was introduced to support the migration of entire virtual data centers across nodes within the cloud. A set of predictive methods, including performance forecasting, were used to optimize online scheduling and facilitate large-scale virtualization in the cloud. In order to obtain accurate performance predictions, a new model was created to measure the impact of resource usage on the power consumption of physical machines, and the relationships between resource metrics were quantified using multivariate regression techniques. Building on this model, two predictive methods were developed: CPU utilization forecasting model and memory consumption modeling. And based on these models, two strategies were devised for the load scheduler: one involved moving entire virtual data centers to nodes with lower energy consumption during periods of low utilization, and the other involved redistributing the components of a virtual data center to avoid hotspots and inefficient resource usage. These techniques were put to the test in a live cloud infrastructure comprising 1000 machines, and the results showed that the new approach could lower energy consumption by 20% compared to state-of-the-art load schedulers.

In various real-world scenarios, factors like weather, traffic or fiscal policy, beyond the agents' control, can impact game outcomes. This analysis demonstrates the effectiveness of this novel concept through a normal-form game example.

Although in-person assessments can reveal vulnerable system components, they may not be effective against covert attacks that bypass detection during prolonged operations. We present a predictive real-time monitoring method for identifying covert attacks on ICS that exploit network traffic manipulation. This strategy employs Pattern Recognition and Time Series Analysis to detect anomalies in system data alongside attack patterns learned from simulated scenarios. Utilizing real-world ICS data from the 2020 International Conference on Industrial, Harsh, and Humanitarian Computing, we demonstrate that our method allows for up to 90% of system states to be tracked in real-time. We also illustrate that our approach can block a cyber attacker after approximately 150 seconds of network traffic manipulation. This capability is made possible by identifying the attacker through our method, which enables proactive policy-making to prevent harm to the system. Furthermore, we demonstrate that prioritizing the learning of certain patterns (such as those related to human operator activity) can yield comparable results. We also outline a strategy for transitioning from simulated to real-world scenarios.

Many companies use a standard framework that measures "average treatment effect" (ATE), but there's a significant challenge to increase its detection power while maintaining "false discovery rate" (FDR) within a predetermined threshold. Popular algorithms like the BH method struggle to control FDR, particularly when encountering positive dependence, which requires conservative estimations. In this paper, we propose new statistical approaches that can reliably and efficiently calculate ATE, demonstrating their effectiveness in both simulated and real-world datasets, which outperform the BH method in terms of efficiency without compromising FDR control. Additionally, our methods allow for improved computational speed using the benefits of sparse data representation. Our work offers practical and efficient statistical tools for ATE estimation that can scale to massive datasets while remaining straightforward to implement.

shifts across various fields like vision, language, and multimedia. Most existing domain adaptation techniques leverage domain-invariant features by utilizing both source and target domain data. However, obtaining target domain data can be challenging, particularly when working with large datasets. This issue is compounded when domain adaptation is taken to a different level – cross-database adaptation – which requires matching features across multiple domains with diverse data distributions. A notable application of domain adaptation in computer vision is image-level adaptation, which involves matching distributions for learning with data from multiple domains. This paper proposes a novel image-level adaptation technique called MDA-SN, which leverages multiple domain adaptation via self-supervised learning and semi-supervised learning. By using variational autoencoders to capture data distributions and batch normalization to eliminate unnecessary details, MDA-SN can generate synthetic images to facilitate downstream tasks like object detection and tracking. Furthermore, MDA-SN can also be used for enhancing model robustness through unsupervised target data simulation during training. The approach is validated through experiments on several datasets including ADIT, DTIT, and iTWKSC, which exhibit diverse distributions and require unique mapping for domain adaptation. The results show that MDA-SN significantly outperforms other approaches in terms of accuracy and robustness.

Deep Space transport is presented, utilizing a cutting-edge Gas Core Reactor (GCR) integrated with a magnetohydrodynamic generator. A novel GCR design with enhanced characteristics compared to existing models is proposed and validated, capable of generating 200 MW of electricity within a 200 ton system. This GCR consists of a spherical cavity within a molybdenum-92 enclosure surrounded by a 50 cm thick liquid beryllium reflector, utilizing a fuel mix consisting of 235 UF4, KF, and K. Numerical simulations reveal the efficacy of this design, producing 206.8 MW of electricity along with 2.6 GW of waste heat at a 2300 Kelvin keff of 1.2584. Additionally, this study involves the performance assessment of various spacecraft configurations powered by the proposed GCR, examining interplanetary transport efficiency. Analysis of rocket propulsion systems reveals that for short missions (less than 300 days), chemical rockets are the most efficient option, whereas for longer missions, nuclear-electric propulsion systems utilizing the GCR for 180 MW of electricity offer improved performance, accelerating the spacecraft by a factor of 30 in mass utilization compared to traditional rockets. Furthermore, this study invesTiates the usage of the GCR's radiation energy output for passenger cancer treatment during the mission, showcasing its potential as a high-yield medical tool in space.

theoretical underpinnings of variable instantiation in Answer Set Programming. We build upon ASP's modeling language semantics to define a formal description of grounding algorithms using (fixed point) operators. Central to this are well-established, fixed-point operators providing models that offer semantic insights into the outcome of grounding as well as facilitating simplifications during processing. We outline the various fixed-point operators associated with ASP and introduce a novel method for defining these operators based on the intuition that non-clausal variables take on values that satisfy the most satisfied dispositions relative to their current setting. We also discuss the connection to previous work focusing on modeling semantics in contrast to grounding. Finally, we provide an overview of an existing tool capable of computing fixed-point models statically, incorporating reasoning capabilities essential for decision-making during the grounding process.

By numerically calculating the boundary-bulk entanglement on small rings and directly comparing it to the bulk entanglement, we conclude that both systems exhibit a positive response to increasing disorder. We extend this analysis through an effective disorder average of the holographic area, confirming that the boundary-bulk discrepancy in the Heisenberg model grows with disorder intensity. Conversely, we found that the boundary-bulk discrepancy in the Majorana Kitaev chain behaves oppositely, decreasing with disorder intensity. We propose that this contrasting behavior arises because the boundary-bulk entanglement in a thermodynamic sense is a measure of order and that the Majorana Kitaev chain's unique properties lead to a disorder-induced enhancement of bulk Poincaré entanglement relative to its boundary counterpart.

waves emanating from the Sun's corona can accelerate electrons, resulting in the formation of type II radio bursts. Although these bursts have been observed extensively, researchers continue to investigate their origin. To address this, we studied a notable solar eruption on October 16, 2015, that involved an EUV jet, a streamer in white-light, and a type II radio burst observed using advanced imaging technologies. The radio burst was imaged by LOFAR, which revealed that the fundamental and harmonic sources of the burst were not in the same location. Accounting for scattering of radio waves due to turbulent electron density, we corrected for this separation, determining the location and speed of the radio burst. The analysis showed that the burst was triggered $\sim$0.5 solar radii above a low-lying jet, propagating at a speed significantly greater than the jet, supporting the hypothesis that a piston shock driven by the jet in the lower corona caused the burst.

its ability to identify patterns in datasets is well-established, albeit limited by the rapid growth of computation time with dataset size. A shift towards quantum computing could potentially resolve this limitation, offering both established machine learning algorithms and novel quantum-based approaches. We present a quantum embedding scheme that not only accelerates pattern recognition but also effectively handles noise. The fundamental principle of this scheme involves encoding input data into quantum states utilizing a Green's function-based basis, where the overlap between basis states determines the similarity of input data. We implement this approach using an experimental setup consisting of superconducting quantum circuits, demonstrating its feasibility and verifying that it operates independently of quantum noise through numerical simulations. The quantum embedding scheme exhibits a linear increase in computation time with dataset size, thereby avoiding the exponential growth seen in classical algorithms. We also demonstrate that this approach can be used to train machine learning models, while numerical simulations indicate its potential to revolutionize pattern recognition by shifting from classical to quantum computing.

"Werewolf," is a party-based competition between two opposing groups. Citizens and mafia members are the main groups. Mafia members possess special abilities that distinguish them from the citizens, who are the dominant group due to their higher numbers. Researchers have developed a mathematical model that represents the game's progression as a discrete-time pure death process. Studies were conducted with a specific focus on even odds in favour of the mafia having their first kill of the night.

Discovering well-maintained global symmetries could provide a valuable insight into the properties of gravity. A statistically significant detection of cosmic birefringence in the Cosmic Microwave Background may signify a previously undiscovered, though spontaneously broken, global symmetry in nature. Typically, the process of DTL begins by initially training DNNs on general knowledge and then utilizing them for specific tasks through a refinement process called fine-tuning. There have been two commonly observed patterns of transferability among pre-trained DNNs: one being that larger gaps between pre-training data and downstream information result in lower transferability and another indicating that transferability tends to decline from the initial to the final stages of DNNs. Nevertheless, these findings were primarily based on natural image datasets, thereby restricting their scope. This work seeks to broaden our understanding of the essence of transferability and discover new insights by conducting a thorough evaluation across a diverse set of fifteen indoor scene datasets comprising human and object-focused images. By utilizing a unique dataset collection that encompasses a wide array of domains, we were able to identify two essential factors contributing to transferability: one being that a larger number of semantic categories and objects shared between pre-training and downstream information result in higher transferability and another indicating that transferability varies significantly among different DNN layers.

Yet, cloud-based services can finish quickly or be delayed significantly, like containerized microservices. As a result, traditional BPE management techniques may lead to excessive idle time, making it necessary to adopt a new approach. To address this, we present a novel strategy called RSO, or Service Orchestration with Relevance, which prioritizes services based on relevant factors rather than execution order. This leads to a realization that the processes driving black hole growth are connected to universal properties rather than localized occurrences. Moreover, the Thakurta metric essentially describes the exterior of a black hole existing within a universe that is homogeneous and isotropic on a large scale. The technique directly relates to fragmentation functions and as such is testable in an off-shell quantum chromodynamic environment without relying on the fragmentation functions' properties in simple case studies. we derive the Poisson equation solution for empty space in a scenario with a rotating gravitational system, analogous to the Sun, and consider the implications of this solution for the behavior of test objects within its gravitational field. The general solution to the Poisson equation, expressed in terms of the distance r and angle θ, is represented as a series expansion of a function F(θ) multiplied by r's power, as well as inverse and inverse-squared terms, along with coefficients that depend on θ. This solution is comparable to the results of Wigner's relativistic treatment of the Schwarzschild solution, which uses spherical harmonics, revealing a fundamental non-relativistic model of the early Earth's rotation and its gravitational effects. Furthermore, we describe how this new solution can be employed to 1) rectify inaccurately calculated perihelion shifts, 9.095 seconds for the non-relativistic model versus 11.6 seconds for the correct calculation, and 2) explain phenomena observed and documented by ancient astronomers, including the skewness of the Earth's equator and its axial rotation's slight length variations.

A spanning tree on vertices of degree at most k is considered as strongly balanced if for every edge in the tree, there exists another edge in the tree, such that the difference between the number of leaves under these two edges does not exceed k. In their research, the authors have shown that any graph with minimum degree k contains a spanning tree that meets this strong balance condition, and they provided an O(k^4 n) time algorithm to find such a tree. 

In our research, we have introduced an O(k^2 n) time algorithm to find a spanning tree that meets a weaker balance condition. Specifically, the tree should satisfy that for every edge in the tree, there exists another edge in the tree, such that the absolute difference between the number of leaves under these two edges does not exceed k. 

In addition, the research also covers the scenario where the tree needs to be sparse, meaning that it should have at most k +1 edges. A well-known algorithm for finding a sparse tree is Rajan's R+ algorithm, but it only guarantees a balance with a desired bound of the size of the largest leaf subtree divided by k. Our research shows that we can improve the balance achieved by R+ with an O(k) factor for any k >= 1.

with the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) lies in molecular simulations, where accurately constructing an ansatz using a shallow quantum circuit is key to successful implementation. Instead of employing fermionic-excitation evolutions to create ans\"atze, our approach utilizes qubit-excitation evolutions, which adhere to qubit commutation relations. By doing so, qubit excitation evolutions can accurately construct ans\"atze, even with a few gates, making them more efficient than fermionic-excitation evolutions. To take advantage of qubit excitation evolutions, we present the QEB-ADAPT-VQE protocol, which is a new VQE algorithm that outperforms the fermionic-activation VQE (FAVQE) algorithm. QEB-APT also surpasses FAVQE in adaptivity during circuit learning, often resulting in circuit success in FAVQE's cost plus one, and sometimes at a lower cost. Our protocol leads to ansatz construction that is generally smaller and more effective, especially with a smaller number of ancilla bits. nonlinear optical systems has been the foundation for significant progress in numerous sectors, including semiconductors, communication, and biology, due to their ability to generate intense short pulses. These systems, though vital, are susceptible to damage caused by intense light, resulting in a limitation known as the average power trade-off. To overcome this limitation, developing methods to prevent and repair damage is essential. We have developed an innovative method - Intelligent MParma - that deeply integrates knowledge of nonlinear optical systems, expert experience, and 1D-CNN network guidance to forecast damage and suggest optimal parameter settings for prevention or repair. Using expert-labeled training data, our model learns to anticipate damage and identify suitable strategies, thereby increasing average power within safety limits. In this paper, we introduce MParma and its initial application, the prediction of damage caused by high-energy pulses in fiber Brillouin amplifiers and suggest potential mitigation techniques.

GPT-2 and GPT-3 can be leveraged for producing high-quality text, however it remains uncertain what exactly GPT-n is learning. A two-part examination aims to illuminate this understanding: Firstly, it investigates how GPT-3 utilizes multi-modal inputs to produce outputs similar to those provided as supervision during its training. A novel metric called MLEI: Measuring output 'looking ahead' and 'looking in' is created to evaluate the degree to which sequenced pre-training methods induce models to incorporate input modalities in generated text. Findings from 8 assessments suggest that GPT-3 tends to integrate input modalities in roughly 60% of the time. Secondly, GPT-3's capacity to act as its own teacher via self-supervision is explored. A framework called GPT-3 Trainer is proposed, allowing for evaluating self-supervised learning in text generation. Findings show that GPT-3 can train itself with notable improvements, however input modalities tend to contribute less to the generated text compared to the target supervision provided.

Initial breakthroughs in the field relied on unsupervised image translation techniques, which required either element-wise or batch statistics to convey encoding information between images. These techniques could not fully capitalize on the self-supervised nature of the task. Progress was made possible by supervised diffusion models, which treat the complex process of generating realistic images as a sequence of increasingly precise corrections. These corrections are learned using both the underlying distribution of real images and the distribution of its generated counterparts, enabling the production of high-resolution images without the need for conditioning on specific inputs or averages. Although challenging to understand and implement, the introduction of new axioms has facilitated the development of more efficient algorithms. These advancements have enabled the creation of images of increasingly high quality, whether given a single input or without a specific task in mind. Notably, the field of statistical diffusion models, which originated in the late 1980s, underwent a period of relatively little activity in the years that followed. Since then, there has been a resurgence of interest in the use of iterative Markov chains as a general purpose tool for a variety of tasks including image generation and denoising. This interest, along with the development of the parameterized Markov process (PMP) theory of diffusion Markov processes in the late 2010s, may ultimately be credited with the breakthroughs that have been achieved in the field. specific prior sampling approach must be used, which involves selecting prior samples that meet a minimum likelihood requirement. Researchers have developed methods like Markov Chain Monte Carlo derivatives for this purpose, which utilize warped Markov Chain proposals to minimize discarding prior samples. Despite their success in various scenarios, these methods have limitations when dealing with highly constrained problems, where the minimum likelihood threshold may be close to the highest possible value. In such cases, Markov Chain Monte Carlo derivatives fail to efficiently sample from the prior. In response to these limitations, we introduce a novel method, the Minimum Threshold Random Walk, which circumvents these issues by implementing random walks with minimum threshold interruptions, thus allowing it to efficiently sample from the prior. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in the context of two specific problems, namely the calculation of the Higgs boson mass in the Standard Model and the rotation matrix coupling constant for the galactic dark matter. Our analysis reveals that the Minimum Threshold Random Walk outperforms Markov Chain Monte Carlo derivatives, producing more efficient nested sampling results.

We calculate a temporal two-particle correlation function and observe oscillations that decline when the model's imaginary Liouvillian gap narrows, a behavior that indicates a transition is imminent. When parameters deviate little from this critical point, our analysis reveals a frequency-momentum space two-particle correlation function dominated by a coherent, low-dissipation superfluid. A substructure emerges within this superfluid, characterized by a frequency shift in the correlation function's spectral density, denoted as $\hbar\Omega_0$. The superfluid's depletion is quantified by an effective wave function coherence length, from which we derive the frequency shift as being influenced by phase fluctuations within the superfluid. A notable outcome of our study is the observation of a sideband structure in the correlation function's spectral density, one which could potentially facilitate coherent, dissipation-induced two-particle tunnelling experiments.

To address these issues, we suggest using a pre-trained transformer model with a learned aggregation strategy to create a semantic mask, which then identifies the degree of semantic similarity between in-distribution and out-of-distribution data through contrastive learning. This method, SemanticCS, can be readily extended to handle various OOD scenarios without compromising the underlining inductive bias of the pre-trained model. Instead, we treat Charisma as a composite of both visual and non-visual attributes that cannot be separated simply. To address this complexity, we propose an end-to-end composite attribute prediction model, focusing on combining visual and non-visual characteristics, while addressing issues such as data imbalance and overfitting. This study tackles the challenge of accurately positioning new objects with no prior knowledge, a step often skipped in 3D reconstruction pipelines. Typically, a single rotation matrix or set of rotation matrices is used to estimate an object's pose, assuming that objects inherently possess a unique pose. However, this method proves inadequate when objects that can be rotated identically (similar orientation) are part of the dataset. This study proposes a novel approach that involves using symmetry groups to represent unique transformations in object pose, a concept commonly utilized in computer graphics for similar purposes. We exploit the fact that different symmetry groups exhibit distinct subgroups and leverage these relationships to create a pose estimator that takes these patterns into consideration. We go on to test our method on the SBS and the SSS datasets, sets containing objects with reflectional and dihedral symmetries, respectively. In doing so, we establish a baseline for these datasets and observe that our method outperforms or rivals the current state-of-the-art results. Additionally, we demonstrate that objects with significant surface distortions can be accurately positioned using our approach.

In an effort to minimize financial losses, major film producers and studios continually seek a more reliable method for estimating movie revenue before making an investment. Researchers in this field face an additional hurdle: the limited availability of a large, contemporary dataset to inform their models. In an attempt to address this challenge, our study proposes a new, comprehensive dataset titled "MPS," which represents the largest public collection of movie props ever created. This dataset includes 850 movies, released over the past 28 years, and offers a range of analytical data such as movie scripts, filming locations, production costs, and props - with each prop featuring a high-quality photo and detailed description. This dataset has been shared publicly and has the potential to transform the movie industry by facilitating innovative applications. In our study, we present two proposed techniques for estimating movie revenue based on the MPS dataset. Our techniques involve the application of deep learning, where the model is trained on props specific to each movie and takes into consideration the number of props, filming location, production costs, and props genre when calculating revenue. Our study shows that the accuracy of our technique is around 95% and sets a new benchmark for box office prediction techniques.

A significant feature of commercial plenoptic cameras, the lenslet array captures spatial and angular light information in a single exposure. This paper introduces a novel, efficient, and scalable architecture utilizing multiple programmable graphics processing units (GPUs) to manage and process light field data. Applications such as disease risk analysis and health resource allocation significantly benefit from categorizing areas based on their health and demographic characteristics. The purpose of this study is to explore the concept of a heat map as a tool for visualizing geographic data and propose an in-depth statistical model that incorporates spatial dependency factors. The research proposes a Bayesian approach combining a Poisson distribution with a Star-Kriging technique for accurately forecasting a range of rare medical conditions across different areas. algorithms for complex systems whose behavior is unknown. This algorithm excels in environments where there is only limited, high-noise data from ongoing experiments. It achieves exceptional results by making the most of various types of secondary information about the dynamics, such as basic physical laws and a basic control strategy. The algorithm essentially finds the best possible solution to an optimization problem by gradually refining a dynamic system model that incorporates unknown components by analyzing trial actions. The model uses advanced mathematical formulas to predict system behavior based on the actions taken so far. The success of this approach was proven under certain assumptions and was further supported by experiments on two critical systems, including a model of how the pancreas regulates blood sugar levels and a model of a sophisticated aircraft, in various simulation environments. These methods perform at least as well as more traditional approaches, in some cases better, and in the specific cases studied, perform nearly as well as if the dynamics were completely known.

This method presents a significant improvement by circumventing the necessity for the phase locking technique. Instead, our approach categorizes time into two distinct frameworks: reference frame adjustment and data transmission. Within the former frame, our approach ensures that the distortion in the phase of the reference frame is considered as an information source. This efficient quantum communication method has immense potential for the implementation of quantum key distribution on a large scale.

As a result, we gain insight into the polaron's ground and excited state properties, and discover that the polaron's effective mass exhibits a non-linear response to changes in the interaction parameters with the surrounding particles. Unlike the original model, where a set fraction of processing capacity is allocated to routine jobs, this extension allows for varying fractions of routine jobs' processing capacity to be assigned on each machine. The model seeks to minimize total costs, which incorporate penalties for task delay and labor fees, against labor capacity constraints. Notably, unlike single-machine settings, it has been found that even the simplest parallel-machine setting with two machines becomes computationally intractable. Therefore, a approximation algorithm focusing on optimizing task assignments has been developed and its accuracy evaluated through a local ratio method. The algorithm's performance was verified by analyzing its outcome in simplified examples. Moreover, an investigation into whether it is possible to improve the solution by processing one task at a time showed that even with this approach, the problem remains NP-hard, thus validating the need for an approximation solution.

This challenge cannot be ignored because soft ground accommodates weight and provides traction, allowing robots to move on surfaces that would otherwise prevent locomotion. A major obstacle in harnessing soft ground for robot mobility lies in accurately predicting the deformation patterns of the terrain. For robots to take advantage of this type of ground, they need to understand their environment, minimizing the uncertainty in their localization and locomotion capabilities. This study introduces a new control approach that not only generates robust and efficient gaits but also helps to mitigate the uncertainty in the robot's state estimation as it navigates through soft ground. This approach utilizes deep learning-based predictive models to understand terrain deformation patterns. An integrated system is presented that combines reinforcement learning for policy development and forward modeling to determine the robot's state, using data collected from a real-time sensor. Our results show that this integrated system yields gaits that are robust and efficient, and significantly reduces the uncertainty in the robot's state estimation.

Given the trend towards implementing security measures via codified policy decisions and exchange of signed, hashed data between devices, it is crucial for firmware updates to be integrated into existing security frameworks. Existing security solutions, however, are inadequate as they either lack or misrepresent firmware update mechanisms. This study introduces a standardized approach to integrating firmware updates into established Security Information Sharing (SIS) frameworks. Our results show that the local self-energy's imaginary component, which governs the decay rate of initially localized states, can serve as a probabilistic phase transition order parameter, facilitating the characterization of critical behavior and multifractal nature in many-body localized states across various disorder intensities. Moreover, we establish that the fractal dimension associated with the local self-energy experiences a discontinuous change at the phase transition, where it transitions from less than two in the localized phase to greater than two in the thermal phase. Furthermore, the local self-energy's asymptotic scaling behavior in the vicinity of the critical disorder strength is nonuniversal, enabling the determination of the critical dimension governing the local self-energy's scaling properties. Moreover, the correlation between the local self-energy and the propagator's nonlocal behavior allows for the prediction that the local self-energy's expectation value exhibits multifractal behavior in the vicinity of the critical disorder strength. Our predictive findings await experimental validation.

In response to these obstacles, this study proposes an alternative approach called HyperIJS, a hierarchical, question-efficient system designed to predict multiple targets simultaneously. The task requires identifying key terms related to the request's technical context, allowing developers to locate relevant sections in the source code and apply the desired changes. This breakthrough reveals that when subjected to these high-frequency sound waves, colloidal gels exhibit a profound reduction in rigidity. Acceptance algorithm traditionally demands complete and ranked preference lists from each party. However, studies show that stable matchings are achieved even with shorter, albeit non-empty, preference lists, suggesting their potential use. This paper investigates the computational needs of finding the first or next stable matching when considering a limited and varied set of preferences. Specifically, when each agent only submits a single-itemed list, we analyze the problem's complexity when it comes to receiving new offers and decide on an optimal response. In particular, the problem of determining whether there's a stable matching and generating such a matching, especially the last one, are systems that can potentially be solved efficiently if the market only needs to consider a limited, $O(\log n)$-sized list. This paper also examines the challenge of creating new preferences when agents only submit a single-itemed list and shows that creating a single, sufficiently long list is at least as challenging in terms of computational needs.

This paper presents a new method called Three-Dimensional Keypoint Detector (3DK), where a single model directly predicts keypoint coordinates from projected oblique camera rays. To facilitate a unified prediction framework, we reformulate the problem of 3D detection as a new keypoint-based representation. We design a model optimization method that treats 3D points as targets, and a loss function that combines the mispositions of direct 3D points and the connections between them. 3DK outperforms previous methods with an effortless simplicity, exhibiting exceptional performance on both direct 3D points and complex multi-point contours, thus demonstrating a more complete 3D representation.

QL using neural machine translation (NMT) models holds great promise for automating complex query generation, but currently faces a significant obstacle: translating SPARQL queries into other languages. Our study develops a novel approach that combines the strengths of both. We demonstrate how to effectively train an NMT model to produce queries in languages other than English by utilizing both English and target language SPARQL queries, along with their corresponding translations. This innovation involves designing a way to align the subject-object relationships within these queries during the training process. We successfully trained an NMT model to translate queries in Portuguese, French, and Spanish, and achieved exceptional accuracy, with the majority of generated queries (95% or more) being correct in at least 95% of their elements. The simplicity and generalizability of our approach makes it suitable for applying to any language pair.

From a theoretical perspective, this research examines how the injective envelope of a given dissimilarity matrix can be used in clustering, including scenarios where the cluster structure is unknown a priori. From a computational standpoint, this research proposes an algorithm to compute a hierarchical clustering structure, called RAGs for Relations and Graphs, which utilizes an explicit representation of the injective envelope of the given dissimilarity matrix to define the cluster structure.

Rendering achieves a balance between computational simplicity and visually realistic

Specifically, we investigated the finite-temperature and zero-field thermodynamics of a single finite dimer cluster and a decagonal cluster model modified from the 120-degree helical compound Ba$_3$Pb$_2$Ge$_2$O$_7$. Due to the large prime number 13 exceeding the typical maximum quantum size, the use of a multi-level cluster Monte Carlo algorithm and a 13-site branching process in our simulation allows for a significant reduction in the effects of a discrete finite basis set for spin and compactification schemes. The results show that these models can be well-characterized by the heisenberg spin Hamiltonian after projecting out low-energy states and that dimer and decagonal cluster models display comparable phase diagrams. Notably, the presence of both solid and liquid phases is only achieved when accounting for the full basis set and incorporating a discrete discrete degree of freedom inspired by recent studies on spin liquids. The simulation reveals two spin liquid phases separated by a first-order phase transition, with the ordered helical phase not observable in the thermodynamic properties due to minimal order parameter within the simulation constraints. The study's findings are expected to be generalizable to similar trimer-based compounds.

PT-3, have exhibited an unexpected capacity for zero-shot learning. Specifically, to accomplish this, users can instruct these models to classify sentiment with untrained examples by prompting them with reviews paired with labels such as "Does the user like this movie?" The model can then be trained to select "yes" or "no" from the subsequent word choices. While zero-shot learning holds the promise of reducing training costs by eliminating the need for pre-defined labels, it is hindered by its slower training pace compared to more traditional supervised learning methods. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach that leverages the natural text for supervisory signals. We demonstrate that our proposed technique, which utilizes two regularization terms, enables faster training and higher performance than traditional supervised learning methods in the context of sentiment classification using GPT-3. To verify the efficacy of our approach, we conducted experiments on both sentiment and event extraction micro-tasks, observing faster training times and better performance on these tasks. Our results reveal that our method can achieve similar accuracy as supervised learning but at a fraction of the cost in terms of the number of training examples required.

a robust first-order electroweak phase transition has been carried out as a prerequisite to studying electroweak baryogenesis within the context of the $Z_3$-invariant NMSSM, considering recent data from the Higgs sector, dark matter searches, and analyses from the Large Hadron Collider involving lighter charginos and neutralinos. This includes thorough reviews of the latest relevant LHC studies. With the assistance of various benchmark scenarios, it is demonstrated that while the LHC has started to exclude parameter regions favoring small $\mu_\mathrm{eff}$ and strong first-order phase transitions, other involved and compatible regions remain unaffected by current LHC results. Furthermore, such an area might be consistent with all theoretical and experimental limitations. We develop a novel metric to measure this potential impact, applying our method to a widely used parameter in vaccine evaluation--the vaccine effectiveness against infection. For Scenario I, II, and III defined by the World Health Organization, we use Bayesian modeling to combine real-world effectiveness and clinical trial data, and assess how conclusions may be affected by uncertainties in vaccine efficacy assumptions. Our findings show that pre-specified criteria for approving COVID-19 vaccines are most vulnerable to changes in assumptions about scenarios where vaccine effectiveness is lowest and immune response is weakest. These results suggest that criteria should be re-evaluated, especially in low-prevalence scenarios. They also imply that vaccine evaluation should be expanded to include broader use of observational data and a more cautious estimation of uncertainty. Finally, our analysis highlights the utility of sensitivity analysis as a proactive tool for identifying potential biases and weaknesses in clinical trials and public health policies, which can be leveraged in future trials to anticipate and mitigate challenges before they arise.

We have demonstrated that central charge, conformal dimensions, and operator product expansion coefficients are encoded in wavefunction overlaps, accompanied by universal corrections that rely on cyclic orbifold CFT content. This approach allows for numerical computation of all conformal data solely based on low-energy eigenstates, a method that was verified in the Ising and XXZ models. Additionally, we used this approach to study the Haagerup model and determined the central charge and lowest scaling dimension of a specific spin-1 operator.

annotation is a crucial task for linguistics and natural language processing, typically addressed through machine learning. Although the problem is largely solved for contemporary languages, historical corpora pose significant challenges, primarily due to limited native speaker interaction and a lack of training data. Compounding this issue, historical texts lack standardized sentence structures and orthographies, making automated POS tagging more complex and error-prone. In light of these complexities, instead of assigning single tags with uncertainty, a novel approach presents a statistical POS uncertainty model that reflects a distribution of possible tags within the word. This model is grounded in the concept of "words know their meanings," initially developed for modern English, and has been adapted and tested on 18th-19th century English texts. POS uncertainty tagging offers a more accurate reflection of the tagging process, while allowing for data-driven tag assignment when necessary. This paper outlines the methodology behind the POS uncertainty model, describes its adaptation for historical texts, and evaluates its effectiveness on several corpora, including the Periodical Work and Thomas Gisborne's Sermons. Additionally, it demonstrates how the POS uncertainty model can be integrated into sequential neural network models, such as BERT, for tagging periods of 18th-19th century texts.

In consequence, our study contributes to the Complementarity Constraint Quadratic Program (CCQP) model, with the aim of identifying the minimum-value attainer within the model's feasible space. To effect this, our method first establishes that any CCQP minimizer, assuming it exists, must be a weakly monotone increasing function. To validate the practical application of our method, our study further establishes the existence of a utility function that satisfies the monotonicity property but may not be differentiable.

Nevertheless, human requirements often lack essential information, or they contain inaccuracies or ambiguities stemming from their verbal description. We develop a novel city planning pipeline that enables the formalization of implicit city planning demands, along with their verification for compliance with existing urban plans. Our system consists of natural language-based components, coupled with a geographic information system (GIS), and utilizes techniques in natural language processing (NLP) along with inductive program synthesis (IPS). This allows our system to analyze verbal city planning demands and integrate GIS-powered data to verify whether these demands can be fulfilled while adhering to existing urban plans. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our system through an experimental evaluation on several datasets. Additionally, we highlight potential advancements in this area, focusing on the incorporation of location-aware IPS models and a more extensive evaluation of the various NLP and GIS data sources available. This incorporates a novel, location-embedded version of the IPS technique, which enables the formalization of city planning demands to be realized in a more locale-specific manner.

Nevertheless, its performance is limited by semantic inconsistencies between datasets. To optimize visual-textual alignment for CLIP models on various tasks, we introduce a technique that refines CLIP's visual outputs via a two-step process: initially, we use a distance metric to separate the compacted visual embeddings into sub-manifolds, and then we realign these sub-manifolds with relevant text embeddings via a distance-based assignment method. This technique is universally applicable and can be seamlessly integrated into existing CLIP fine-tuning procedures. Our experimental evaluations on four image datasets (Steklo, CUB-200-2011, Cars-196, and SOP) and two medical segmentation datasets (MS-CTSC and MSCI) demonstrate that our method enhances model performance on these datasets.

This approach involves modeling a function with a continuous probability distribution, typically a Gaussian process (GP). By leveraging GP properties, researchers can establish a correlation between function outputs and input variables, facilitating a deeper understanding of the relationship. Although widespread, GP-based inference can be computationally intensive, requiring the resolution of challenging equations. This dissertation presents an in-depth investigation of using numerical solvers to address these inference challenges. It begins by examining the fundamental limitations of each solver and its impact on parameter sampling. A comparative analysis of three solvers is conducted, with synthetic data sets used to evaluate performance and real-world applications assessing practical effectiveness. Furthermore, this research strives to provide insights that are applicable to a broad range of computational models, emphasizing generic algorithmic principles that can be applied beyond Gaussian processes.

pathology and radiology is undergoing significant transformation.  Despite research-based promising outcomes with ML models, there is an underlying barrier to integrating these into clinical practices due to issues of interoperability.  The DICOM standard provides specifications for the representation, storage, and exchange of digital images and related information but the standard's complexity hinders the adoption of ML-based image diagnostics.  Therefore, there is a need for simplified imaging information exchange model that can facilitate the communication between various ML models and clinical environments, and the DICOM framework appears to be an ideal candidate with its established global usage.  In this study, we propose I3D-DICOM, a framework that includes a lightweight imaging modality and a coding system designed to simplify data capture and exchange.  By testing the framework's efficacy, we aim to contribute ML's transition from research to clinical practice in the field of imaging diagnostics.

Clebsch canonization has been proposed to convert Lie-Poisson equations into equivalent canonical equations using Lie groups and their associated quotient spaces. This method provides a combination of the generalized Eulerian coordinates with coordinates from group elements and their coset representatives. We exemplify this method using the Lie-Poisson equations related to the symmetric tensor coordinates of the Lie algebra $so(3, 1)$ and the SU(2) * SU(2) *... * SU(2) cosets, which are subsequently reinterpreted as canonical equations in Eulerian coordinates using ghost variables, resulting in equations of point vortex dynamics and the physical Hamiltonian of the Wess-Zumino term.

Neural Networks (DCNNs), are capable of generating robust image representations, but are limited when dealing with orientation transformations. To address this limitation, we have developed a Novel Rotation-invariant Large-scale Evolution (NRLLE) approach. By utilizing unsupervised rotation detection and a mutation-based method, we have successfully evolved sparse DCNNs with rotation-invariant properties on large datasets. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of NRLLE in producing robust deep features that remain invariant to image rotations, thereby facilitating improved performance in downstream tasks. Our experiments involve using DCNNs to extract features from the DCNN-L layer, followed by a lightweight Classification Head to classify images. Our method achieves consistent accuracy across different angles of rotation (0, 120, and 240 degrees) on the UT-Mahnoor and UT-Mahnoor-Ext datasets, with an accuracy of 93.22%, 73.87%, and 63.57% respectively. Furthermore, we have adapted and applied NRLLE to the real-world task of detecting glaucoma from Fundus Face View Fundus Finger print images, resulting in a high area under the ROC curve of 0.9921 on the unique Glaucoma dataset.

-19 is a combination of symptoms and laboratory data analysis. However, gathering symptoms information naturally for a patient involves answering a series of questions is a more natural approach than providing laboratory data from various sources. Consequently, a multi-task learning model has been proposed, incorporating question answering and laboratory data interpretation to enhance accuracy in diagnosing COVID-19. This involves training a BERT model on combined natural language questions and laboratory data, and then fine-tuning it using a supervised learning approach based on labeled diagnoses and laboratory data. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model yields a substantial improvement in accuracy relative to sole diagnostic methods relying on questions or laboratory data, achieving an error rate of 0.073. Furthermore, the model's performance on laboratory data alone is substantially higher, at a rate of 0.087 compared to the previous best achievement of 0.087, when solely relying on QA. Moreover, the proposed model produces a diagnostic output in the form of a probability distribution over possible diagnoses similar to the probabilistic nature of the previous best achievement.

a measure of association in statistical analysis. The strength of evidence for linear correlation is often evaluated using a hypothesis test, resulting in a p-value. Under certain data transformations and assuming a specific probability distribution, a t-statistic provides an approximation of the p-value. This study examines how effectively the t-statistic approximates p-values in non-normal linear associations, using various types of data that are normally distributed or not. The results suggest that the t-statistic's accuracy in detecting linear relationships depends on factors such as data set size, non-normality level, and the degree of linear correlation present. Furthermore, research outlines conditions under which the t-statistic's p-value approximation is accurate and develops a correction formula that yields better results, particularly when working with small data sets or non-normal data. Overall, this work aims to provide a better understanding of when and why the t-statistic's p-value approximation of Pearson's r works (or doesn't) and proposes an improvement to these p-values in certain situations.

an increase in research on explainable recommendation systems. Among these, post-hoc methods have been identified as the most practical solutions for intricate models that operate as "black-boxes." We introduce an effect where the medium is warped by the motion of charged particles in a way that the Larmor formula accurately describes the energy lost due to radiation. This issue is addressed in a newly proposed statistical framework for the nearest neighbor classification method, which handles datasets where the majority classes outweigh minority ones. By utilizing a two-stage process, where we first detect objects in combined catalogs and then verify candidates in individual source catalogs, we develop an effective method for quasar discovery. This collaborative strategy facilitates the discovery of highly luminous, distant quasars even in data sets with limited right ascension coverage. As a result, we isolate 236 new ultra-bright quasars at redshifts above 4.8, including 219 luminous quasars exceeding a brightness of 22nd magnitude and 17 extremely luminous quasars exceeding a brightness of 24th magnitude. Furthermore, our analysis reveals 8 new quasars at redshifts above 6 with luminosities exceeding 22 magnitudes, as well as 8 new quasars at redshifts between 5.5 and 6 with very high luminosities, achieved through black hole pair evaporation theory limitations. Lastly, our findings lead to an enhanced far-UV luminosity distribution that significantly surpasses a normal Gaussian curve, even when data from different redshifts are combined.

By utilizing a superconducting qubit coupled to a quantum dot via a highly controllable gate, we took advantage of the existing Josephson oscillator mechanism to directly detect low-frequency signals resulting from the quantum dot. As the temperature continued to drop, we also noticed a shift in the quantum dot's energy level due to the exchange of Cooper pairs, further verifying the presence of a quantum dot-superconducting island system. In a clinical trial involving 23 participants with known scoliosis, the robotic approach was compared to manual scanning by systematically moving an ultrasound probe along the spine to identify the vertebral level with the highest curvature. Average scoliosis levels were similar across both techniques (68.96 degrees vs. 67.39 degrees). Although vertebral levels of the highest curvature differed significantly (P < 0.01), the robotic approach reported results in less time (23.4 s) compared to manual scanning (41.1 s), requiring fewer control commands (four vs. six). Moreover, the robotic experience was perceived as positive by participants (average score: 83.10%), supporting its potential as an automated scolosis assessment tool. Further research is required into ultrasound image quality, exploring the potential for the robotic approach to provide automatic scoliosis level measurements and vertebral curvature level identification.

Unlike traditional approaches that rely on a single mean duration per phone class, this technique allows for accurate modeling of inter-phone variability and context-dependent duration. We assessed the effectiveness of various models, including BERT and SPACY, when using different labeling schemes and datasets. To address this issue, we propose a new, more effective MIMO structure that eliminates interference by isolating the subnetworks' outputs. Besides issues related to structure, temperature, and support bearings, one major factor behind elasticity is the backlash in the transmission systems. This study proposes a method for improving trajectory precision using supplementary sensors and a novel feedback control strategy in combination with a feed-forward approach based on flatness.
